planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, humus-heavy woodland soil in shade to deep shade; unlike most Smilax it has no tendrils and rarely climbs, so treat it as a colonizing woodland-floor groundcover rather than a trellis vine.

directions: Upright carrionflower is a thornless, herbaceous Smilax of rich deciduous woodlands from the Great Lakes south to Texas and east to the Appalachians, distinguished from its relatives by weakly climbing to fully erect stems that lack tendrils entirely. Small dioecious umbels of greenish-yellow flowers open in late spring with a faint carrion scent that draws fly pollinators, followed by blue-black berries that persist into fall for birds. It spreads gradually from a thickened rhizome to form loose colonies on the forest floor, making it a good low-maintenance filler beneath native shrubs and canopy trees rather than a true climber. Divide dormant rhizomes in early spring or fall and leave undisturbed once established.

planting.note: Plant root divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in shade to part shade near shrubs or a fence where the tendril-climbing vine can scramble upward.

directions: Florida carrionflower is a thornless, tendril-climbing Smilax of rich, shaded hardwood forests and bottomlands across the southeastern coastal plain and piedmont. Its small, globe-shaped umbels of greenish flowers carry a mild carrion scent that attracts fly pollinators in spring, and female plants follow with dark berries valued by woodland birds. It dies back to a tuberous rootstock each winter and resprouts reliably each spring, scrambling over low shrubs and brush rather than smothering them. Use it as an unobtrusive naturalizing vine along a shaded woodland edge or fence line where it can be left undisturbed.

planting.note: Plant root divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil in full to partial shade, siting it where the glaucous leaf undersides can be appreciated against a dark backdrop.

directions: Downy carrionflower takes its name from the fine white powdery bloom coating the undersides of its leaves, a distinctive feature among the eastern carrionflowers that sets it apart at a glance from the glossier-leaved Smilax herbacea and S. lasioneura. This thornless, tendril-climbing perennial grows from a tuberous rootstock in rich mesic woodlands and floodplain forests of the central and eastern United States, dying back each winter and resprouting in spring. Small greenish-yellow umbels with a mild carrion scent appear in late spring, followed by blue-black berries that persist for fall and winter birds. Grow it scrambling over low shrubs at a shaded woodland margin and leave the rootstock undisturbed once established.

planting.note: Plant tuber divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade next to a fence, shrub, or small tree the twining stems can climb.

directions: Fourleaf yam is an eastern North American native twining vine, easily told apart from the similar Dioscorea villosa by its heart-shaped leaves arranged in distinctive whorls of three to seven (most often four) along the stem rather than alternately. It grows from a hard, knotty underground tuber, sending up slender, non-aggressive twining stems each spring that climb by wrapping rather than by tendrils or rootlets, making it a gentle companion for a shaded fence or shrub rather than a smothering vine. Inconspicuous greenish flowers appear in loose drooping clusters in early summer on separate male and female plants, followed by small three-winged seed capsules on female vines. Grow it in dappled to full shade in consistently moist woodland soil as an unobtrusive native screening vine.
